William II died 1 May 1278; 'Charles succeeded him without opposition' under the Treaty of Viterbo (24/27 May 1267) and ruled through the bailli Galeran of Ivry: the Villehardouin principality becomes an Angevin possession, same state, same colour (rule 2). Angevin suzerainty itself dated from 1267.
Charles II 'granted the Principality to Isabelle of Villehardouin upon her marriage with Florent of Hainaut' (1289): Villehardouin-Hainaut princes under Angevin suzerainty.

region.text: Corinthia, the Isthmus and the castellany of Corinth

ledger.note: Corinth, mortgaged to Nerio Acciaioli by Angelo Acciaioli after 1365 and 'confirmed' as hereditary in 1371 by Philip of Taranto; the Pope called Nerio 'lord of the town of Corinth' in November 1372. The counterpart is the future Acciaioli Duchy of Athens (Nerio duke from 1385/88); until then Corinth was a fief held of the Angevin prince, so the date marks the start of de facto separation. [Reviewer eu-05-d, 2026-10-19: counterpart was 'duchy-of-athens', which ends in 1311; the Nerio I Acciaioli page: Angelo 'soon mortgaged it to Nerio, who established himself in the town', Philip of Taranto 'confirmed Angelo's hereditary right to Corinth in 1371', and in November 1372 the Pope called Nerio 'lord of the town of Corinth'.]

'In 1383, Achaea was annexed by Charles III of Naples' and 'the Vicary government began' under the Navarrese Company (entered the Morea 1378), 'the reigning power in Frankish Greece'; princely rights sold to Pedro de San Superano 1396.

The Achaean fief ended. [Reviewer eu-05-d, 2026-10-19: counterpart was 'duchy-of-athens', which ends in 1311; the vassal is the fief itself, which per the Lordship of Argos and Nauplia page 'remained in the possession of the de la Roche and the Brienne dukes of Athens' after 1311, passed to Guy of Enghien in 1356 and was sold to Venice on 12 December 1388.]

notes:
Cliopatria rows: the Principality of Achaea row (1206-1439) starts a year late (1205) and ends seven years late (1432). Its 1206-1235 shapes give the Franks the whole peninsula at once, although Corinth fell only in 1210, Argos and Nauplia in 1212 and Monemvasia in 1248; the 1260 shape (minus Laconia) starts two years before the 1262 handover. Two gaps, 1279-1293 and 1326-1384, are presumably drawn under the House of Anjou-Sicily row (the Angevin kings were princes of Achaea 1278-1289 and 1322/1332-1383): new keyframes keep the principality continuous and the anjou dossier should draw the Morea as a vassal tint, not as its own land. The 1314-1325 shape folds in the Cyclades (the Duchy of the Archipelago's row ends 1313) and keeps Karytaina and Akova after 1320. The 1385 and 1395 shapes (c. 14,000 km2) are too large by half: by then the Byzantine despots held Laconia, Kynouria and most of Arcadia, Nerio Acciaioli Corinth, and the Argolid went to Venice and Theodore I in 1388; from 1418 only Chalandritsa, Arcadia (Kyparissia) and the archbishop's Patras remained (new keyframe 1418). The last shape (248 km2, Kyparissia) is right but should end in 1432.

Suzerains of Achaea (rule 4, to be recorded by the suzerain's dossier with counterpart principality-of-achaea): Kingdom of Thessalonica 1205-1209 (Champlitte 'under the suzerainty of the king of Thessalonica'; Geoffrey I made it 'the direct vassal of the Latin Empire'); Latin Empire 1209-1267 (nominal after 1261 under Baldwin II); Venice, nominal, by Sapienza 1209; Charles I of Anjou and the Angevin kings of Sicily/Naples from the Treaty of Viterbo (27 May 1267) to the sale of the princely rights (1396/1404), the king himself being prince 1278-1289; the kingdom-of-thessalonica and latin-empire dossiers of this group carry the first two. Achaea's own vassals, recorded in the ledger: the lordship of Argos and Nauplia under the dukes of Athens (1212-1388; Guy I also owed homage for Thebes), the Duchy of the Archipelago (1248-1278) and the triarchs of Negroponte (1262-1278). Corinth passed to the Acciaioli as an Angevin fief (1365/1371) and is recorded as a loss to duchy-of-athens with confidence 1.

Gaps (confidence 1-2): the Byzantine advance in Skorta during the 1290s (Saint George in Skorta) and Theodore I's gains in Messenia in the 1390s are not on the pages opened; the exact date Lacedaemon was lost after 1264; Araklovon (1213) and the baronies' internal boundaries. Disagreements: Monemvasia Frankish 1248 (Principality and William pages) or 1225 (Monemvasia page); the ransom cession late 1261 (William page) or 1262 (Mystras, Prinitza pages); Geoffrey II's dates (main page 1209-1245 is garbled); Centurione's end 1430 (infobox) or 1432 (death). Pages that would not load: 'Byzantine-Latin wars'. Counterparts without dossiers: Leo Sgouros (Greek lord of Nauplia, Argos and Corinth c. 1198-1208) and Oliverio Franco (Glarentza 1418-1421) are used as name strings; the Despotate of the Morea (1349-1460) is carried inside the byzantine-empire row.

Gazetteer names used as coordinates because the gazetteer lacks them: Andravida, Glarentza, Chlemoutsi, Chalandritsa, Kyparissia, Methoni, Koroni, Mystras, Monemvasia, Grand Magne/Mani, Cape Malea, Lacedaemon, Karytaina, Akova, Argos, Nauplia; the regions Laconia, Argolid, Elis and Messenia are drawn as polygons. Pelagonia is drawn as the Mogila, Bitola and Prilep admin-1 units.
